stops.name: Rome, two years of writing, the Desconhort
stops.campa: Ramon settles in Rome through 1295 and into 1296, working the halls of a curia that has cycled through Celestine V's brief and disastrous reign into Boniface VIII's, petitioning each in turn for language schools, for a standing military order to hold the Holy Land, for anything at all beyond the polite hearing every clerk in Rome has learned to give him. Out of the frustration of these years he writes the Desconhort, the Book of Discomfort, a bitter dialogue between an old fool and a hermit who tells him bluntly that no one will ever believe his Art was given him by God.

stops.name: Paris, the second stay, the war on Averroes
stops.campa: Ramon returns to Paris in August, this time to fight a battle he judges as dangerous to Christendom as any Saracen sword: the teaching, inside the very faculty of arts he had once courted for allies, of Averroist doctrines holding that reason and revealed faith may each be true on their own separate terms, with no need to reconcile them. Against this Ramon sets treatise after treatise arguing, by the Art's own mechanism, that faith and reason are one necessary demonstration and cannot be split apart, a fight he will return to Paris to renew twice more in the years still left him.

stops.name: Barcelona, the king's license to preach in synagogue and mosque
stops.campa: Home again in the Crown of Aragon, Ramon obtains from King James II a document few missionaries before him have carried: royal license to enter the synagogues and mosques of the king's own realms and preach there directly to Jews and Muslims living under Christian rule, compelling their attendance if need be. It is the domestic twin of the African missions, proof that Ramon's design was never only for the distant Saracen but for the unconverted living inside Christendom's own cities, and it gives legal shelter to years of preaching he will carry out in Barcelona, Valencia, and Majorca between the longer voyages abroad.

stops.name: Majorca, the Cant de Ramon, the old man's own accounting
stops.campa: Home on the island through a long quiet year, Ramon writes the Cant de Ramon, fourteen stanzas of six eight-syllable lines that walk his whole life past the reader: the conversion, Miramar, the Art, the roads and the refusals. It is the troubadour craft of his worldly youth taken up again and turned to the only lady he now serves, and it is not a boast. He complains in it, plainly, of how little his labor has come to, and asks God for protection and for intelligent companions to carry the work he cannot carry alone much longer.

stops.name: Cyprus, Famagusta, the mission to the Latin East
stops.campa: Nearing seventy, Ramon takes ship again, this time east to Cyprus, last major Christian foothold within easy reach of the Levant, its port of Famagusta thick with Genoese, Venetian, and Frankish merchants trading into a Mamluk-held Holy Land no crusader army now holds. He preaches among the mixed Latin, Greek, and Syrian population of the island, tests his Art on whatever learned Muslims and schismatic Christians pass through the port, and begins to press the case, which will occupy his last decade, for a mission to the Tatar khans of the Asian mainland, whose conversion he believes might outflank Islam entirely.

stops.name: Port Ayas, the Armenian coast, the embassy to the Tatars
stops.campa: From Cyprus Ramon crosses to Port Ayas on the Cilician coast, the chief harbor of the Christian kingdom of Lesser Armenia and the western terminus of the overland road to the court of the Ilkhan in Persia, where embassies and merchants pass constantly between the Mongol world and the Latin one. Here, closer to the Tatars than any earlier stage of his life has brought him, he composes the Rhetorica nova, an art of persuasion meant to travel with missionaries as far as the steppe itself, before turning back west, his hope of reaching the Great Khan's own court still years, and several voyages, away.

stops.name: Montpellier, between missions, the Book of the End
stops.campa: Back on the Montpellier road after Genoa, Ramon writes the Liber de fine, the Book of the End, laying out in cold administrative detail exactly how a crusade ought to be financed, manned, and directed if Christendom would only listen: standing military orders merged into one, a tithe on the clergy, a fleet built and kept ready rather than raised anew for each disaster. He is past seventy and has buried, in these same years, most of the popes and princes he first petitioned as a younger man; still he drafts the plan again, on the theory that the right argument, offered often enough, must eventually find the right ear.

stops.name: Bugia, the public sermon, the stones and the chains
stops.campa: Now past seventy-five, Ramon sails to Bugia on the Barbary coast and, as at Tunis fourteen years before, preaches the Trinity openly in the public square. A mob gathers, stones him where he stands, and drags him before the qadi, who this time does not commute the sentence to expulsion outright but has him chained and thrown into a cell for half a year, debating faith through the bars with a Muslim scholar the Latin calls Homer in an exchange he will later set down as the Disputatio Raymundi christiani et Homeri saraceni, before the city's authorities finally put the old man on a ship bound home.

stops.name: At sea, the wreck off Pisa
stops.campa: The homeward ship from Bugia founders in a storm within sight of the Tuscan coast; Ramon, chained by age and weakness now as much as by any Saracen jailer, is pulled from the wreck along with what survivors the sea allows and put ashore near Pisa rather than at Genoa or Majorca as intended. He has survived a death sentence, a half-year's imprisonment, and a shipwreck within the space of two years, and takes the accumulation, as he has taken every earlier trial since the visions in his chamber, as proof that his work is not yet finished and God is not yet done with him.

stops.name: Pisa, the Ars brevis finished, the crusade renewed
stops.campa: Recovering at Pisa, Ramon puts the Art into its final and most compact form, the Ars generalis ultima and its short companion the Ars brevis, the version students after him will actually use, having pared away four decades of revision to the working core of the wheels and the Dignities. He also renews, from his sickbed, the old campaign for a new crusade, addressing the Pisan authorities and any Genoese captain who will listen, unwilling to let a shipwreck stand as the last word on a plan for the Holy Land he first drafted for Pope Nicholas IV twenty years before.

stops.name: Montpellier, the crusade treatise renewed
stops.campa: Back at Montpellier, Ramon drafts yet another crusade memorandum, this one timed for the general council Pope Clement V has summoned and twice postponed, where Ramon means to be heard whenever it finally sits. He is seventy-seven, has been refused by popes and princes across four decades, and shows in these last petitions no sign of the fatigue his body must by now be carrying; the wheels of the Art, he insists to whoever will still hear him, prove the case for the recovery of the Holy Land as certainly as they prove any article of the Trinity.

stops.name: Paris, the last stay, thirty works, the doctors' approval
stops.campa: Ramon returns to Paris in November for what will be his longest and most productive stay, dictating some thirty treatises against Averroism and in defense of the Art over two years. In February of 1310 the masters of arts and medicine, for the first time in his long acquaintance with the schools, put their names to a letter certifying his teaching as sound; the chancellor follows the year after, declaring the Lullian doctrine in accord with the Catholic faith, and King Philip the Fair writes commending him. It is the nearest thing to victory Ramon will ever have from a university that argued with him for twenty years.
